articles.title: Missed opportunities lead to deflating Illinois loss to Purdue
articles.summary: Purdue claim the Cannon trophy in 24-17 win during Illinois homecoming.
articles.body:
CHAMPAIGN, Ill – In a sold out Gies Memorial Stadium during homecoming week, fans were not treated to the usual Illinois, Purdue shootout that we've seen in recent years. Instead they got a low scoring game with no real excitement until near halftime.

Illinois had laid claim to the Cannon trophy two seasons in a row, but after the 24-17 loss, Purdue is now in possession of it for the time being.

Saturday evening, all eyes were, of course, on the defense. After last week's loss to No. 7 Ohio State, defensive coordinator Bobby Hauck let head coach Bret Bielema know that he would be departing the program after just four games.

Linebacker coach Roger Cooper took over the defensive play calling duties in this game. Cooper, in his first season with Illinois, was brought in alongside Hauck from Montana, and head coach Bret Bielema is confident that he can keep the 3-3-5 formation as competitive as possible.

"If anything wasn't ever where Bobby couldn't call it, I would go to Coop naturally. Brought him in, made sure he was good with the plan," Bielema said. "I think we'll continue to make some modifications, some tweaks on defense, but for us right now just stay healthy."

The Illinois defense wasn't spectacular in this one, but it showed flashes in the first half by getting timely stops in the red zone and forcing field goals. It definitely wasn't perfect though. Early in the second, WR Asaam Waseed broke free for a 61-yard catch and run after a blown coverage from the Illini secondary.

The defense was able to settle in a bit after a flag pushed Purdue back, and got off with just a field goal allowed. This foreshadowed the touchdown to come later in the quarter as WR Tra'Mar Harris broke down his man and brought in a 21-yard TD, the first of the game.

It was Illinois' offense that was uncharacteristically quiet the entire game. The Illini didn't score until the 0.21 second mark of the second quarter. And who else but WR Colin Dixon to get the ball rolling for the Illinois offense.

The much needed score energized the entire stadium. In a four minute drive, QB Katin Houser and the Illini were able to find success in short yardage passes and rushes.

To keep the drive alive on 3rd and 2, and to put Illinois in the red zone, Houser ran it himself for 14 yards and the first down. What followed was the 7 yard Dixon score, giving him his eighth of the season and just two away from tying the single-season record.

The success on offense was very short lived though.

Some bizarre playcalling and unfortunate penalties caused multiple missed opportunities for the offense. The most puzzling moment in the game happened with just 13 seconds left in the third quarter.

A solid drive put the Illini in the red zone with a chance to make it a one score game. Instead, on 3rd and 3, offensive coordinator Barry Lunney decided to call a Jordan Anderson rush, which got immediately shut down for a loss of two yards.

Instead of taking the field goal, the offense stayed on the field on 4th and 5 which resulted in an incomplete pass. The offense has been keeping the Illini afloat all season, but Bielema knows execution in critical moments needs to be better.

"Our offense has done a lot of really good things," Bielema said. "But, Duke, Ohio State and this game, our three losses, the inability to make some 4th-down plays or some 3rd-down plays when we were in 4-down territory or 4-down scenarios , has been the tell of that."

To add insult to injury, early in the fourth, Illinois put together a good drive in which a deep ball to Dixon resulted in a pass interference, putting the offense into Purdue territory. What followed was a 34 yard catch and run from WR Ty Robinson for the touchdown.

The fans' excitement was very short lived, as a holding penalty nullified the touchdown and backed Illinois up even farther. The cherry on top, Houser was sacked for a loss of 9 yards, ending the promising drive on 4th and 20.

"I think it just comes down to executing. We felt really good about our plan, we just didn't get it done execution wise, which I feel like is a common theme for us this year," Dixon said. "Like after a lot of the games we look back it's like we didn't execute and this is the result."

Illinois missed out on 10 points, which could have easily shifted the tide in the game. The nail in the coffin, Houser's third interception of the season. Bielema knows this could have been handled better, but notes Houser is capable of growing this.

"Even when they scored a touchdown to make it the 2-score game again, we have 3.5 minutes, 3 timeouts and we don't need to throw a ball down the middle of the field there desperation-wise," Bielema said. "It'll be a really good learning moment for Katin, for our offense."

Despite the relatively low scoring affair, there were still some highlights that are worth checking out.

RB Antonio Harris rushes up the middle to give Purdue a 24-10 lead. This essentially sealed the game for the Boilermakers.

Katin Houser throws his second TD of the game, this time to Ty Robinson. This made it a one score game, but it was too little, too late.

Ryan Browne: 18-27 passing, 255 yards, 1 touchdown

Asaad Waseem: 3 receptions, 98 receiving yards, 61 yard catch

Colin Dixon: 10 receptions, 116 receiving yards, 1 touchdown

Illinois now sits at 2-3 and is below 0.500 for the first time this season. Some serious discussions will have to be had about the future of this team. Can the defense readjust to the departure of Hauck? Will the offense bounce back? Its next opportunity to bounce back is Oct. 10 against Michigan State.

articles.title: Dwayne McDougle's pick-6 turns game Nebraska's way in a 48-23 victory over Maryland
articles.summary: (AP) — Dwayne McDougle III's 81-yard interception return for a touchdown sparked Nebraska in the first half, and the Cornhuskers all but shut down Maryland a...
articles.body:
LINCOLN, Neb. (AP) — Dwayne McDougle III's 81-yard interception return for a touchdown sparked Nebraska in the first half, and the Cornhuskers all but shut down Maryland after that in a penalty-filled 48-23 victory Saturday.

The Cornhuskers (5-0, 2-0 Big Ten) are out to their best start since 2016 with defending national champion and sixth-ranked Indiana coming to Memorial Stadium next week.

The Terrapins (2-3, 0-2), a week removed from a 54-3 home loss to UCLA, led most of the first half before seeing the game turn on the third pick-6 thrown by Malik Washington over four quarters. Their 18th loss in 20 Big Ten games only increased the pressure on eighth-year coach Mike Locksley.

Without injured running back Jamal Rule, quarterback Anthony Colandrea had the first 100-yard rushing game of his career, going for 108 on 10 carries. He was 26-of-39 passing for 238 yards and three touchdowns. Kwazi Gilmer had career highs of 11 catches for 147 yards and two TDs.

Washington was 23 of 44 for 254 yards and a touchdown, and his two interceptions increased his season total to six, all in the last two games. Chris Durr Jr. caught seven passes for 149 yards and a TD.

The Huskers were down 23-14 midway through the second quarter when McDougle stepped in front of Washington's pass intended for Kaleb Webb and ran it back all the way for Nebraska's longest pick-6 since 2007. Washington's three pick-6s over four quarters are most over such a short span since Kyle McCord threw three in the first two quarters against Pittsburgh on Oct. 24, 2024, according to Sportradar.

Colandrea passed one yard to Luke Lindenmeyer to finish a quick eight-play, 80-yard drive that put the Huskers in front 28-23 at half, and Gilmer's TD catches of 5 and 30 yards pushed the lead to 25 points.

Maryland piled up 300 yards of offense in the first half and just 62 the rest of the way.

Maryland: The Terps are doing nothing to help themselves. They were called for two personal fouls, a silly unsportsmanlike conduct when kick coverage player Zion Elee was caught shoving after the whistle on a touchback and roughing the passer. They were 1 of 14 on third downs and are a combined 2 of 30 over the last two games.

Nebraska: The Huskers have scored at least 30 points in each of their first five games for the first time since 2014 in spite of being penalized 16 times for 132 yards, the most since they were flagged 16 times for 145 yards against Texas A&M in 2010.

The combined 28 penalties were the most in a Bowl Subdivision game since Florida Atlantic and Western Kentucky totaled that many in 2021. The 247 penalty yards were most of any game this season.

The teams combined for 18 penalties in a first half that lasted 2 hours, 4 minutes. It was the most penalties in a first half since San Diego State and California combined for 19 on Sept. 14, 2024, according to Sportradar.

Colandrea wowed the crowd early in the third quarter when he jumped high over Lavain Scruggs along the right sideline halfway through a 15-yard run. Colandrea coverted the third down and got up with a bounce.

Maryland visits No. 5 Ohio State next Saturday.

Nebraska hosts No. 6 Indiana next Saturday.

articles.title: 100 years reborn, Ryan Field opens to wows and a deafening din
articles.summary: As the sun set over Evanston on Friday, a golden glow emanated from the limestone exterior of Ryan Field, which was mobbed for the first time by the Wildcat...
articles.body:
As the sun set over Evanston on Friday, a golden glow emanated from the limestone exterior of Ryan Field, which was mobbed for the first time by the Wildcat faithful.

Inside, a montage of moments from Northwestern University's long path to rebuilding its football stadium played across the video screens. It featured Pat Ryan Sr., the benefactor behind the new stadium, and other Northwestern stalwarts extolling how the "most user-unfriendly" college arena had become the very opposite.

The video closed with two poignant words, especially for a school that's used a temporary lakeside stadium for two years: "Welcome home."

Soon, the lights turned down, and the speakers blasted "Thunderstruck." A deafening roar, from the standing-room-only student section no less, seized Ryan Field when the football team made its entrance. The Wildcats had, at last, come home to their new home.

The explosive entrance was the culmination of a centurylong journey which began when the former stadium hosted its first game exactly a hundred years prior, on Oct. 2, 1926.

It hadn't always been a smooth one. When the university pitched the new stadium, which it also plans to use as a concert venue, some nearby residents in this leafy northern corner of Evanston revolted.

That rumpus went unmentioned by Friday's montage, of course, but the video did remind fans that Northwestern has weathered tougher challenges before — certainly in the early '80s, when the football team's ignominious winless streak threatened to put Northwestern's future as a Big Ten member in question.

Now, on a most beautiful day in Evanston, those worries were history. The new $875 million Ryan Field, long hyped to become America's best place to watch football, had opened. And Ryan himself saw the opening as a challenge to all new stadiums to come.

"We set a new standard," Ryan told the Tribune ahead of the game.

Demolition of the old Ryan Field began in February 2024. Aiming to make way for a stadium opening in little more than two years, crews soon made the Wildcats' hulking citadel vanish, starting with the rust-ridden structure beneath the bleachers.

The old stadium opened on Oct. 2, 1926, and "the Purple," as the Tribune called the team, blanked South Dakota. It got its first name, Dyche Stadium, a month later. And it seemed to have an auspicious future, since the university had once dreamed of building Dyche into a massive, triple-deck stadium.

Yet even as built, the stadium rarely reached capacity, a challenge eventually compounded by the foundering product on the gridiron. And Dyche, too, decayed. So in 1995 — which wound up being the Wildcats' watershed Rose Bowl season — Northwestern started to envision a big renovation.

The touched-up stadium opened in 1997 with a new name: Ryan Field, in honor of the man who had spearheaded the project.

A couple of decades later, however, Ryan Field gamedays often seemed sparse. The age of the place revealed itself in the discolored bleachers where sometimes few people sat. It felt empty.

Enter Ryan and his wife, Shirley Ryan, once again.

In 2021, the couple donated $480 million to the university, including money for Ryan Field's redevelopment. The next year, Northwestern revealed its design for a smaller but more comfortable stadium that could also host commercial, non-NU events.

Nearby residents soon became incensed about the prospect of massive concerts that could funnel sound into their backyards. The decision on whether to enable Northwestern's plans came down to Evanston's City Council, which in October 2023 tied at a preliminary vote.

Mayor Daniel Biss broke that tie in favor of the university. Weeks later, the council gave its final approval along similar lines. It also approved a pact with Northwestern, which promised $150 million in benefits to Evanston residents.

"In politics it is always easier to say no," Biss said Friday, when he briefly visited the stadium. "And I'm really glad that we didn't fall prey to that here, because this is a beautiful facility. And I think it's one that's going to bring a lot of joy to people across Evanston for a long time."

Biss, who said he would not stay for the game, hurried toward the exit after he cut the ribbon alongside the Ryan family.

Northwestern's Dave Davis, the longtime liaison between the university and residents, stuck around and mingled with the big names who had gathered there. He insisted that he talks to the neighbors "every day" and that Northwestern's benefits pact will bolster the city.

It's a contention that one neighbor, Matthew Grayson, disputed as he stood, hands on his hips, looking toward the other side of the new stadium. Music echoed from Ryan Field. Many of his neighbors had left their homes Friday to avoid the game, he said.

"It's an example of how Northwestern does whatever it wants to do," he said with a pronounced dismay.

Another neighbor stood on Asbury Avenue with a more opportunistic stance. Christian Piekos, a former WLS-Ch. 7 reporter who moved into a home near Ryan Field six months ago, held a cardboard sign hawking gameday parking.

He's excited about the new stadium. He'd gotten one taker for parking thus far. And he planned to attend the game.

Back on the other side of the stadium, people streamed toward the gates. Mustard's Last Stand, the hot-dog stand right next to Ryan Field, tried to entice some of them with a food cart by the sidewalk.

"I've been worried and nervous," said the stand's co-owner, Lonnie Starkman. "We've been doing this for so long that we know what we're doing. But you never know, you know. It's opening day after two years of not having a game."

It succeeded mightily. "Extremely well," he said, as fans packed into Mustard's small building.

Oh, and Starkman shares his birthday with Ryan Field.

Next to Mustard's is the parking lot where the longest-tenured Northwestern fans tailgate. Some donned sequin-embroidered purple hats and Willie the Wildcat T-shirts.

They were all excited about the new stadium, marveling at its cornucopia of amenities.

"It's worth the cost," Park Ridge resident Darryl Krall said.

Krall said he's been a Northwestern tailgater for the better part of 45 years. He plans to be here for the next 45.

Bob Guth, a class of 1972 graduate and a 44-time season ticket holder, thinks that attending the game is just as much of a "social experience" as it is one to watch semi-decent football.

And surviving the team's 34-game losing streak from 1979 to 1982 was no easy feat, he added with a laugh.

"We've got four or five guys here that I went to school with back in the '70s," he said. "We don't see each other often, so it's more about the renewal of relationships."

There was plenty more food behind the gates. Mustard's now has an outpost inside Ryan Field, too, part of an all-out effort by Northwestern to attract Chicago, Evanston and North Shore restaurants to the new stadium.

One member of what's billed as the "Great Chicago Food Festival" is Frontera, an extension of chef Rick Bayless' restaurants. He runs the original Frontera Grill and the Michelin-starred Topolobampo in Chicago, among others.

Ahead of the game, Bayless reclined in a seat as he took in the new arena's cavernous but comfortable confines. "One of the most stunning stadiums in the world," he said. Especially because of the dining options.

"It's very egalitarian," he told the Tribune. "You could come here and enjoy food that is from all of these great chefs in town, and you don't have to spend an arm and a leg. That, sort of, is the Chicago way. That we're regular people."

Much of Frontera's menu was not available, however, since the stand didn't have heat yet. Bayless said he would hand out guacamole and chips instead. "We decided to just be very magnanimous," he added, chuckling.

Construction on the stadium had not been entirely completed by gameday, with a few of the finer details remaining on the to-do list. It was still easy for many fans to marvel at everything the crews had accomplished in the span of two years.

The NFL-style stadium's white canopy hangs over all 35,000 fans (around 12,000 fewer than the old stadium could fit), sitting in actual seats instead of bleachers. Except, that is, for the newly ferocious student section, in which fans physically cannot sit.

Students must stay standing, ready at any moment to back-kick the metal plates behind them. And as they discovered at a student preview event the week before, under the instructions of hypeman Joe Spivak, the Wildcat Wall can produce a terrifying din, loud enough to confound the foe.

When the lights turned low and "Thunderstruck" began blasting, the Wildcat Wall knew exactly what to do.

And perhaps they did vex the once-formidable Penn State Nittany Lions.

Northwestern got off to a hot start in the first quarter. First, a field goal. Then a touchdown. The Wildcat Wall erupted into "Go U Northwestern" for the first time.

In the second quarter, Penn State notched its first touchdown, but the Wildcats' ground game quickly clapped back. That didn't faze the Penn State fans in attendance, yet.

"I feel like they have the momentum right now, but eventually it's going to wear off," said Keith Landberg, who had traveled from Florida to watch the game. "And Penn State will win."

And would Ryan Field beat out the Nittany Lions' home? "Not even close." He allowed that the "loudness is there" at the new stadium. But he saw little comparison to Beaver Stadium, whose 100,000-plus capacity makes it one of the largest stadiums of any kind in the world.

Indeed, because Northwestern finished the first half up 24-7. The Wildcats and the Wildcat Wall were not finished.

"You give them something easy to do like the wall, and they're all gung-ho for it," said Sam McLain, a senior at Northwestern, referring to his fellow students. "But I also think making a bunch of people stay standing for the game also really helps that. Northwestern has a bad habit historically of being game-sitters."

McLain is a diehard Wildcat, but in an unorthodox way: He became well-known on campus as the "Highlighter Kid" for wearing neon-colored outfits to basketball games.

But on Friday, he wore a purple-and-white shirt. It was too important an occasion.

Northwestern announced the game had sold out, but many tickets ended up on the resale market. It seemed that some of the upper reaches of the stadium had empty rows.

And in any case, as Northwestern kept padding its lead, the seats started to empty.

Not so for the Wildcat Wall, which stayed put until the end.

The Wildcats ran up the scoreboard to 34-13. A line of security guards stood below the Wildcat Wall, apparently expecting to hold back any students who wanted to storm the field.

When the game finally wrapped, the football players rushed toward the Wildcat Wall, giving high-fives to the students in the front row.

Fireworks exploded over Ryan Field, and a light smoke filled the stadium as the celebration continued.

At the press conference afterward, in the underbelly of the new stadium, coach David Braun spoke, awe-struck, of gratitude for the Ryan family, the student section and countless others.

And of manifesting dreams, "the best dream of my life."

"I'm telling you right now," Braun said. "Nights like tonight are nights that you pray for."
authors: Shun Graves, Claire Murphy, Chicago Tribune

articles.title: 3 Matchups to watch between the Vikings and Dolphins in Week 4
articles.summary: The Vikings will need to exploit individual matchups to beat the Dolphins in Week 4.
articles.body:
The Minnesota Vikings appear to have advantages across the board heading into their Week 4 matchup against the Miami Dolphins . Brian Flores has led the Vikings' defense to the league's top unit in EPA/play allowed and DVOA. Minnesota has the best overall special teams, which also rank first in DVOA.

Even the Vikings' offense could pop off if Kyler Murray gets settled in. Minnesota currently ranks last in offensive yardage, but even without Justin Jefferson on Sunday, the offense still boasts Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings, T.J. Hockenson, and a solid offensive line.

Winning individual matchups will be key to a potential Vikings victory. Below are three key matchups to watch where Minnesota could hold a massive advantage, tilting the scales heavily in its favor.

3 Matchups to watch between the Vikings and Dolphins in Week 4

Jordan Addison vs. Chris Johnson/ Jason Marshall Jr.

The Vikings' offense was largely ineffective last Sunday against the Buccaneers , but Addison was one of the few bright spots, catching five passes for 90 yards and a touchdown. There were other potential opportunities to get him the ball, but whether because of pressure or indecisiveness, Kyler Murray turned them down.

Addison caught two of three targets 20+ yards downfield, displaying big-play ability even with Jefferson sidelined with an ankle injury. Can Minnesota test that again against a defense allowing 9.1 yards per pass? Johnson, Miami's first-round pick, has allowed 11 completions for 123 yards and two touchdowns on 16 attempts. Marshall has given up nine completions for 92 yards on 10 attempts in coverage, per Next Gen Stats.

No one has produced more pressures than Turner this season (25, per NGS), and his 3.5 sacks are tied for sixth in the league. Turner has lined up on the offense's left side on 55% of snaps this season, meaning he will likely line up primarily against third-year left tackle Patrick Paul on Sunday, a formidable player who stands 6-foot-7 and weighs 325 pounds. Per PFF, Paul has allowed six pressures and one sack, and his 90% pass-block win rate is tied for 16th in the league, per ESPN.

Turner isn't the only EDGE rusher with the potential for a big day. Van Ginkel has three sacks this season, and his 12 pressures tie for 20th in the NFL heading into Sunday. He will likely primarily line up across from right tackle Austin Jackson, who has allowed a team-high 12 pressures and two sacks, per PFF. Jackson has a 39.6 pass-blocking grade from PFF, the lowest among all tackles who have played at least 135 snaps this season.

Flores could still line Turner up across from Jackson to create another mismatch. Van Ginkel and Turner's impacts will be vital not only to sacking Willis but to keeping him from escaping the pocket. With De'Von Achane on injured reserve, Willis (17 carries, 101 yards, one touchdown) is the Dolphins' leading rusher among healthy players.

articles.title: Winners and losers from FSU’s statement win over Virginia
articles.summary: Florida State rolled past Virginia 38-7 behind a huge day from Ashton Daniels, a dominant defensive front and a much-needed win for Mike Norvell.
articles.body:
Florida State entered Saturday needing something more convincing than simply another win. The Seminoles delivered it. After falling behind 7-0 and producing just 38 yards in the opening quarter, Florida State scored 38 unanswered points to rout Virginia 38-7 at Doak Campbell Stadium.

The victory improved FSU to 3-2 overall and 1-1 in ACC play. From Ashton Daniels' record-setting afternoon to a defensive front that overwhelmed Virginia, here are the biggest winners and losers from Saturday's win.

Daniels was responsible for all five of Florida State's touchdowns and made some history along the way. The FSU quarterback rushed 17 times for 136 yards and five touchdowns, setting the program's single-game record for rushing scores.

His biggest play came on an 81-yard touchdown run in the third quarter that blew the game open and extended Florida State's lead to 31-7. Daniels also threw for 183 yards, giving him 319 yards of total offense.

There wasn't much to criticize after the final three quarters, but Florida State's start certainly qualifies.

The Seminoles managed just 38 yards in the opening period while Virginia accumulated 101 and took a 7-0 lead. FSU opened the game with three consecutive punts before finally finding its footing with a 98-yard touchdown drive early in the second quarter.

There may not have been a more surprising development Saturday than what Florida State did to Virginia up front.

The Seminoles entered the game with seven sacks through four games. They finished Saturday with 10 sacks and 12 tackles for loss, with nine different defenders recording at least half a sack. FSU held Virginia to only 37 rushing yards and 205 total yards while limiting the Cavaliers to 2.8 yards per play.

It was an emphatic response from a defense that had struggled to consistently create pressure during the opening month.

Virginia entered Saturday with an experienced offensive line, yet Florida State made the group look overwhelmed for much of the afternoon. After scoring on its first possession, Virginia never reached the end zone again.

Quarterback Beau Pribula was sacked 10 times, and the Cavaliers finished with only 37 rushing yards when sacks were included. Virginia converted just 3 of 15 third downs and failed on all four of its fourth-down attempts.

Few people associated with Florida State needed Saturday's result more than Mike Norvell. Much of the conversation surrounding the Seminoles throughout the week centered on Norvell's future after a 2-2 start, with his job security becoming a national storyline entering a critical stretch of the schedule.

Instead of allowing that pressure to build, Norvell's team delivered its most complete performance of the season. Florida State didn't merely upset the Cavaliers; it overwhelmed them, scoring 38 unanswered points in a 31-point victory.

One win will not erase every question surrounding the program, but beating a favored Virginia team in convincing fashion was exactly the type of response Norvell needed with scrutiny surrounding his tenure.

Danzy continues to give Florida State an explosive element in the passing game.

The receiver led the Seminoles with 70 receiving yards and played an important role in helping the offense find its rhythm after the slow start. With Virginia forced to account for Daniels and the rushing attack, Danzy helped punish the Cavaliers when opportunities developed downfield.

articles.title: Chicago Bears expected to start quarterback Tyson Bagent vs. New York Jets: ESPN source
articles.summary: The Bears are expected to start Tyson Bagent at quarterback against the Jets after he took the majority of first-team reps at practice, sources told ESPN and...
articles.body:
The Bears are expected to start Tyson Bagent at quarterback against the Jets, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

While coach Ben Johnson did not publicly disclose who would start in place of Caleb Williams in Week 4, sources told Rapoport that Bagent took the majority of first-team reps at practice during the week . Case Keenum will serve as Bagent's backup against the Jets.

The video in the player above is from a previous report.

Williams was ruled out for a second straight game as he recovers from a Grade 2 hamstring strain. His recovery timeline is expected to be three to four weeks, according to Rapoport and ESPN's Adam Schefter.

Bagent's last start came in 2023 in a 16-13 win over the Carolina Panthers, which is 1,059 days removed from Sunday. He started four games his rookie season while former Bears quarterback Justin Fields dealt with a thumb injury. Chicago went 2-2 during that stretch.

Bagent sustained a concussion late in the fourth quarter of a 9-3 loss to the Minnesota Vikings on Sept. 20 after Williams left the game with injury . Bagent did not clear the concussion protocol until last Sunday and practiced only once leading into the Philadelphia Eagles game , thus why he did not start in Week 3.

But not long after the Bears earned their second win of the season, Johnson reiterated that Bagent was named the backup quarterback at the end of training camp "for a reason."

Johnson said midweek that the Bears knew the "direction" they want to go at quarterback but that the hot-hand conversation with Keenum would play a part in the evaluation.

"There is such a thing as playing the hot hand," Johnson said Friday. "That is real. We're certainly taking that into consideration. And yet, there's a body of work that goes into it as well. There's a lot of factors at play, and we certainly have talked about it as a coaching staff. Honestly, it's split. If you just ask each coach one-on-one what they think, it's split. I don't know that there's necessarily a right answer or a wrong answer in terms of how we go about this thing. Both of them are well prepared to play and win a game for us here, so I'm excited about that."

Bears LT Braxton Jones on IR; Theo Benedet to start vs. Jets

Chicago Bears left tackle Braxton Jones has been placed on injured reserve after sustaining an injury to his right knee against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 3.

Jones was classified as "week-to-week" and did not practice ahead of the Bears' Week 4 matchup with the Jets. He is eligible to return on Nov. 2 at Seattle.

Theo Benedet, who spent the first three weeks in a rotation with Jones, will start at left tackle, per coach Ben Johnson.

Sunday could be the first time this season that Ozzy Trapilo is active for a game. Trapilo, who started six games at left tackle for Chicago as a rookie last season, worked his way back from a ruptured patellar tendon this offseason far sooner than the Bears had anticipated but was inactive against the Panthers, Vikings and Eagles.

"We're still working out Ozzy just to make sure that the confidence is back," Johnson said. "He's looking better each and every week. He was one of those guys in Wednesday night's practice in pads. He stood out in a good way."

articles.title: Missouri football sets record in dominant win over Florida
articles.summary: The Missouri football program set a cool record against Florida on Saturday.
articles.body:
No. 25 Missouri had its way with No. 8 Florida at home on Saturday.

The game was tied more than halfway through the second quarter before Missouri took over. Missouri scored 10 points in the final four minutes of the half to take a 20-10 lead into the break, then outscored Florida 25-7 in the second half to win 45-17.

Tigers quarterback Austin Simmons went off, throwing for 340 yards and two touchdowns. Running back Jamal Roberts was also no answer for the Gators' defense, finishing with 24 carries for 211 yards and three touchdowns.

This win was so big for Missouri that it set the program record for the largest win against an AP Top-10 opponent.

Sep 26, 2026; Starkville, Mississippi, USA; Missouri Tigers head coach Eli Drinkwitz looks on during the first quarter against the Mississippi State Bulldogs at Davis Wade Stadium at Scott Field. Mandatory Credit: Petre Thomas-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Missouri suffered its first loss of the season to Mississippi State last Saturday, 31-24. Missouri was up 24-17 going into the fourth quarter before allowing 14 unanswered points.

The loss dropped the program to No. 25 in the country, and a loss today would've dropped the team outside of the AP Top 25. Instead, the team played its best game of the season to get to 4-1 overall and stay mathematically alive in the SEC title race.

The Tigers will try to make it two wins in a row next Saturday when it hosts Texas A&M. A kickoff time has yet to be announced.

articles.title: Alex Golesh explains Auburn football's fourth-down miss vs Tennessee
articles.summary: Auburn football saw momentum swing when it didn't convert a key fourth down late against Tennessee. Here's what Alex Golesh said about the decision.
articles.body:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — Facing fourth down, needing a yard to convert and trailing by just three points, Auburn football went for it.

The only thing? Auburn was on its own 24-yard line, and there were nearly seven minutes remaining in what'd eventually be a 24-14 loss to No. 17 Tennessee on Saturday, Oct. 3, at Neyland Stadium.

It looked a lot like the same play Auburn used to ice its win against Vanderbilt a week prior, pitching to Jeremiah Cobb as he hit the edge. Against the Commodores , it was a 21-yard gain. The Vols, however, snuffed it out and went on to score a game-sealing touchdown.

Head coach Alex Golesh explained the decision postgame.

"The thought is, the pictures they had shown, that they would chase it off the backside edge," he said. "We thought we could go hat for hat with Sig (Cody Sigler) and then put Cobb in space. It sucked a little bit being on the left hash there, being tucked up against the sideline, but that was the thought process there."

Asked if there was any concern about running quarterback Byrum Brown up the middle in that instance, Golesh said "that thought didn't necessarily cross my mind," in large part because Auburn talks through those circumstances throughout the week.

"That was our plan on fourth-and-1 in a got-to-have-it-type situation to go to the play we went to," Golesh said, "and I felt good calling it, to be honest with you."

articles.title: Brexton Busch Gives Command For Kyle Busch Classic
articles.summary: Brexton Busch delivered the command for the Kyle Busch Classic at the Las Vegas Bullring.
articles.body:
The Las Vegas Bullring was the site of the Kyle Busch Classic on Friday night to honor the late two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion. Prior to the on-track action, there was a special pre-race command.

Brexton Busch, Kyle and Samantha Busch's 11-year-old son, delivered the most famous words in motorsports prior to the start of the Kyle Busch Classic. Brexton competed in the Legends cars event in his green and orange No. 18 machine.

Kyle Busch, who passed away suddenly on May 21 after a case of pneumonia progressed into sepsis, was a native of Las Vegas. He cut his teeth racing at the Bullring in his early years and captured two track championships.

Brexton Busch Delivers Command For Kyle Busch Classic

Prior to rolling off fifth for the Legends race, Brexton Busch delivered the command for the Kyle Busch Classic. The 11-year-old also waved the green flag for the ARCA race at the Bullring. On X, Brexton wrote :

"Let's go racing at the Bullring!!!!! I start 5th in the upcoming Legend feature, tune in on @FloRacing !

Brexton Busch spun out at one point during the Legends race but ultimately recovered to finish the event. On Thursday, the young Busch finished runner-up in his bandolero car.

Busch told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that he was fortunate to see the race honoring his late father come to fruition.

"It's really cool to see my dad's race come alive. I start fifth. Hopefully I can win it. It's going to be a fun one. "It's really cool to see how many people are here. I bet it's going to inspire a lot of people. The new repave is awesome," Brexton said .

Sunday's NASCAR Cup Series race at Las Vegas will be filled with many tributes to the late Kyle Busch. Kyle's older brother, Kurt, will serve as the honorary pace car driver to begin the 267-lap race.

Kyle Larson, who rolls off sixth for Sunday's race, is piloting a Kyle Busch-inspired yellow and blue paint scheme recognizing Busch's early NASCAR Cup days driving the No. 5 Chevrolet for Hendrick Motorsports.

Kurt Busch Speaks on Kyle Busch Classic, Memorial Rock

Just outside the Las Vegas Bullring stands a memorial rock for Kyle Busch, something the track recently put on display to honor the late champion. Older brother Kurt took to X with a family photo in front of the display and wrote :

"Thank you race fans for coming out and supporting the Kyle Busch Classic at the bullring. Last night was full of emotions and memories of years past. The future looks bright!

Kyle Busch won seven NASCAR national touring series events at the Las Vegas Motor Speedway, including the 2009 Cup Series race.

articles.title: Monroe County Region high school sports roundup for Saturday, Oct. 3
articles.summary: Monroe swimmers win Monroe County Girls Swimming Championship, Milan's Evelyn Gill named Swimmer of Meet; Monroe County Region sports roundup.
articles.body:
MILAN – Erin Dowen set a goal when she took over as Monroe's girls swimming coach five years ago.

She wanted to see her team win the Monroe County Championship.

At the time that seemed a bit ambitious.

"I don't think anyone other than Milan has ever won it," Dowen said.

That changed as Monroe rang up 573 points to overwhelm the field on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026.

"It feels great," Dowen said. "My first year we were dead last and I think we scored less points than what we won by today."

Dowen's Trojans were 112.5 ahead of runner-up Bedford led by freshman Karis Beaton, who narrowly missed state qualifying times in winning the individual medley in 2:17.08 and the backstroke in 1:02.21.

She also led off Monroe's winning 200 freestyle relay, which also included Morgan Kleinow, Blayne Lynch and Sophia Smith.

Smith won the 50 freestyle and was second in the butterfly.

Kleinow was second in the 100 and Andie Eby, Emma Boyd and Ava Dowen posted third-place finishes.

"We had a lot of fast swims," Dowen said.

Bedford coach Holly Scheffer said the same thing.

"We have improved greatly," she said. "We swam awesome today."

Sydnee Knaggs wpm the 100 freestyle for the Mules and was second in the 200. Bedford got thirds from Kendra Bland and Samantha Smth.

Evelyn Gill of third-place Milan was named Swimmer of the Meet after winning the 200 (2:01.3) and the 500 (5:17.88) and swimming with Afton Presley, Kenleigh Vandergrift and Ashtyn Bergstrom on the winning 400 relay.

"I am really happy," Gill said. "I loved swimming with all my friends in the relay."

She also loved keeping the Swimmer of the Year Award in Milan after former teammate Mary Kate Wayne won it the last two seasons.

"We were very close," Gill said. "It's awesome to follow in her footsteps."

Milan could not compete with the depth of Monroe and Bedford, but won two of the three relays and four individual events. Also taking first for the Big Reds were Kaylin Brown (diving), Avery Hovatter (butterfly) and the medley relay of Afton Presley, Tori Kimberly, Hovatter and Ashtyn Bergstrom.

Jillian Layman of fourth-place Dundee won the breaststroke in 1:12.86.

Airport's Ella Baker finished sixth, Maliah McKibben of Bedford eighth, Iva Ravindra of Bedford 17th and Zoey Smalling of Monroe 31st.

Tanylei Neff, Erie Mason : Finished 26th for Mason's best showing in the Clay Invitational. Maddie Kolbe was 30th.

Jack Dunwoody and Wyatt DelValle, Gibraltar Carlson : Took second and third individually to lead Carlson to first place in their own Marauder Invitational. Also finishing in the top 30 were Cam Varner of Bedford (7), Colton Childress of the Monroe Milers (10), Gavin Rohr of Monroe (15), Hunter Rodak of Airport (20) and Mason Martin of Milan (26).

Caleb Healey, Erie Mason : Took third place in the Clay Invitational to help his team finish third. Teammate Porter Ravary ran seventh.

"Her serving was phenomenal." Alexa Turner, Allie Ruhlig and Avery Yaeger also stood out on Senior Night for the 17-1 Kestrels.

Addison Hill, Whiteford : Filled up the stat sheet with 20 assists, 12 digs and 4 aces in a 25-18, 25-19, 25-19 sweep of Morenci. Jordyn Opatrny led with 9 kills and Avery Welch racked up 34 digs for the 14-7-2 Bobcats.

Grêmio will return to action in the Brasileirão next Wednesday (7), when they visit Remo in a clash between two teams currently in the competition's bottom four.

And coach Renato Gaúcho is counting on the kind of "mini preseason" he got because of the FIFA international break as a key factor in getting Tricolor to bounce back.

" This time was essential, because we needed to train a little bit of everything in every area. Physical work, tactical work, technical work, a new coach, the group getting to know our work. Me getting to know some players, some characteristics of some players I still didn't know. Getting to know the academy boys better. So it was important ," he told Grêmio TV.

After the draw with Palmeiras, the squad had three days off before reporting back on September 24.

The Grêmio coach believes the period dedicated exclusively to training has already had an effect.

" We will definitely improve, and we have improved in every aspect as well. A football player has a lot of things the club provides for him. So what I ask of them in return is total commitment on the pitch. Of course, there's a tactical, technical and physical side, but there has to be commitment. It doesn't matter whether he plays 10 minutes, 20 minutes, 45, 90 minutes. He has to give everything, he is paid for that. I've already made that very clear. Any player who doesn't give everything will go to the back of the line ."

Currently 17th with 29 points, Grêmio will visit the 19th-placed side, who have 23.

They need to win and hope Vasco (16th with 31) slip up to leave the bottom four as early as Matchday 29.

articles.title: Adrian College football done in by costly mistakes in homecoming loss
articles.summary: Adrian College football remained winless in the MIAA on homecoming despite Braiden Whitaker's big day. Here's how it happened.
articles.body:
ADRIAN – Moments before the kickoff of Adrian College football's homecoming game, every spectator inside Docking Stadium directed their gaze toward the press box. No, they weren't looking at the dashing media members sitting comfortably enjoying their pregame chicken tenders.

Rather, they watched as members of the Misty Blues Skydiving team descended from the blue sky above to deliver the official game ball to the field.

Their landing — smooth as silk — was in stark contrast to the product the Bulldogs presented on the field.

Adrian never found a rhythm, falling 17-12 to Calvin on Saturday, Oct. 3, in a game riddled with self-imposed errors. The Bulldogs were penalized eight times for a total of 70 yards in the loss.

"We had a hard time getting the flow together," head coach Joe Palka said. "It's just undisciplined football offensively and we just can't tolerate it. We're going to have to take a hard look at that and that kind of stuff's going to have to get cleaned up."

Calvin opened the scoring after getting an early defensive stop. The Knights drove into Adrian territory and kicker Sal Ruffino converted a 43-yard field goal.

On the fourth play of Adrian's drive, quarterback Jake Wright found wide receiver Braiden Whitaker on a deep shot across the middle for a 58-yard touchdown. The Bulldogs took a 6-3 lead after the extra point was blocked.

After two punts, Adrian used a goal-line stand to halt a 21-play Calvin drive that spanned almost seven minutes and 94 yards. Despite forcing the turnover on downs, a three-and-out, followed by a quality punt return, again set the Knights up in good field position.

With 29 seconds remaining in the first half, quarterback Thomas Vaccaro connected with wide receiver Luke Michmerhuizen for a 10-yard touchdown, giving Calvin a 10-6 halftime advantage.

The Bulldogs' missed extra point came back to haunt them in the third quarter. Trailing by four points, Adrian elected to leave its offense on the field on fourth-and-short in the red zone. A deflected pass put an end to a 14-play drive.

The Knights used the momentum from that stop to their advantage. Calvin responded with an 87-yard drive, capped off by a 37-yard touchdown pass to a wide-open Hunter Hogan, extending its lead to 17-6.

Adrian cut the deficit to 17-12 in the final minute, thanks to another touchdown pass from Wright to Whitaker. The Knights recovered an onside kick attempt to seal the victory.

Braiden Whitaker, WR, Adrian – Whitaker hauled in 11 catches for 158 yards and two touchdowns. The Bulldogs' receiver has recorded more than 100 receiving yards in three of his last four games.

Riley Dunbar, WR, Adrian – Dunbar snagged eight catches for 60 yards for the Bulldogs.

Thomas Vaccaro, QB, Calvin – Vaccaro went 23-for-37 passing for 211 yards and two touchdowns. The Knights' signal caller also led the team in rushing with 70 yards on 11 carries.

Luke Michmerhuizen, WR, Calvin – The Knights' wide receiver finished with a team-high eight catches for 86 yards and a touchdown.

"I told the team in the locker room that it's not going to get any easier," Palka said. "You just have to keep fighting. You have to keep working every day. The football gods tend to level things out and hopefully something falls in our favor as we work to get better and improve on what we saw today."

Adrian falls to 2-3 (0-2 MIAA) on the season. The Bulldogs will be off next week before traveling to Holland to face rival Hope on Oct. 17. Adrian's next home game will be on Oct. 24 against Trine.

articles.title: UND starts poor, then piles on points against Murray State
articles.summary: Oct. 3—GRAND FORKS — Perhaps as expected, UND quarterback Jerry Kaminski spent the fourth quarter Saturday afternoon wearing a headset and signaling plays to...
articles.body:
Oct. 3—GRAND FORKS — Perhaps as expected, UND quarterback Jerry Kaminski spent the fourth quarter Saturday afternoon wearing a headset and signaling plays to his backup quarterbacks.

How the Fighting Hawks arrived at this scene, however — completely unexpected.

No. 5 UND let Murray State score the first 21 points of the game before answering with 55 unanswered points en route to a 55-28 victory over the Racers on homecoming in front of 10,985 at the Alerus Center.

With UND looking lifeless early, Kaminski ignited the rally with his arm and legs. He finished with a career-high 98 rushing yards and 186 passing yards, plus a combined four touchdowns.

Kaminski, who hasn't thrown an interception in the last three games, now has 19 touchdowns this season to two interceptions.

"There wasn't ever a splinter of doubt going through my head," said UND linebacker Ethan Boll, a Crookston native. "I have so much confidence in what Jerry and his group can do. It was 'So what? Now what?' I was just thinking we have to find a way to get off the field and get the ball back in Jerry's hands."

UND's offense could share the blame in the bad start, though. UND's first three possessions included a Charles Langama fumble, a Kaminski fumble and a three-and-out.

The two turnovers and a three-and-out resulted in a Tyrell Campbell 8-yard touchdown run, a Mykell Allen 2-yard touchdown run and another Allen 2-yard touchdown run.

With about 12 minutes left in the first half, the Racers led the Fighting Hawks 21-0.

"There's never doubt and not looking at guys with fear in their eyes," Kaminski said. "The offense put the defense in tough situations. We never lost confidence in the defense. We know they're going to bounce back. Guys were confident on the sideline."

The comeback started on UND's next drive. After picking up a fourth down thanks to a pass interference call on a deep ball from Kaminski to Korey Tai, UND scored on the next play. Kaminski found tight end Nathan Hromadka for a 26-yard score to cut the lead to 21-7.

After a Murray State three-and-out, UND needed four plays to trim the lead again. Kaminski ran in from 38 yards out, utilizing a stop-and-start shake around the 10-yard line to deke out a defender and cut the lead to 21-14.

The Hawks tied the game quickly, too. After a three-and-out thanks to a Braden Mohr sack and a Boll third-down stuff, UND's Cameron Weir took a punt 57 yards to a touchdown.

"Cam's return flipped the whole game," Kaminski said. "He comes to work every day and puts his head down and doesn't complain. He's came alive the last couple weeks. We knew that was going to happen right from spring ball. He's super dynamic. When you get the ball in his hands, you expect good things."

Despite trailing 21-0 with 11:55 left in the first half, UND went to halftime with the lead after a Kenten Laughman 22-yard field goal in the final seconds of the half.

UND then scored on all four drives of the third quarter. After stopping Murray State on fourth down in Racer territory, UND countered with a 3-yard touchdown pass to Grand Forks Central product Tray Kuntz.

Moments later, Weir scored his second touchdown of the game — a 17-yard pass from Kaminski to make it 38-21. On Murray State's next play, the Racers fumbled. UND's ensuing play was a 26-yard Langama run for a touchdown and a 45-21 lead.

"Obviously, not a good start for us," UND head coach Eric Schmidt said. "Credit Murray State coming in and giving us a problem defensively. Took us until we could get off the field with our guys a bit to talk about adjustments. We have to do a better job emphasizing holding onto the football. Defensively, we have to respond better and force field goals. The overall demeanor on the team was we had some confidence yet, even though it was 21 points. I thought Jerry's series where we put it on him to get to 21-7 ... after that, we had our footing and got our ball back to our offense."

The Fighting Hawks improved to 5-1 and 2-0 in the Missouri Valley. UND travels to Northern Iowa next week. The Panthers were on bye this week and are coming off an upset of Illinois State last weekend.

articles.title: FSU football report card: Ashton Daniels, Seminoles earn high marks
articles.summary: The Seminoles may have found their groove. FSU crushed Virginia 38-7 behind Daniels' record-breaking performance.
articles.body:
Florida State football finally delivered the complete performance it had been searching for all season.

After a sluggish start, the Seminoles dominated the final three quarters on Oct. 3, rolling past Virginia 38-7 at Doak Campbell Stadium for their first ACC victory of the season. Behind a record-breaking five-touchdown performance from quarterback Ashton Daniels and a suffocating defensive effort that produced 10 sacks , Florida State improved to 3-2 and showed signs of becoming the team coach Mike Norvell envisioned entering the season.

See the best moments from FSU football vs. Virginia

Daniels turned in his most dynamic performance as a Seminole, making his biggest impact with his legs rather than his arm.

The senior quarterback rushed for 136 yards and five touchdowns, breaking the school record for rushing touchdowns in a single game at Doak while finishing just short of the program mark for rushing yards by a quarterback. His ability to create explosive plays on the ground consistently stressed Virginia's defense and fueled Florida State's offensive surge.

This was the version of Daniels that Norvell and the coaching staff envisioned when he arrived in Tallahassee: decisive, explosive and capable of taking over a game.

There is still room for improvement as a passer. Daniels continues to struggle with deep-ball accuracy and timing throws under pressure. His biggest mistake came in the second quarter when he threw behind Jayvan Boggs, resulting in an interception. Still, Daniels completed 12 of 19 passes for 183 yards and more than made up for the turnover with his record-tying effort on the ground.

As of now, this was Daniels' best performance in garnet and gold.

Florida State's offense looked stagnant early but quickly found its rhythm after the opening quarter.

The Seminoles wore down Virginia's defense with a punishing rushing attack, finishing with 465 total yards, including 281 on the ground while averaging 6.1 yards per carry.

Ousmane Kromah helped spark the turnaround with a powerful third-down run in which he broke multiple tackles and pushed Florida State into favorable field position. Shortly afterward, a long screen pass to Tre Wisner set up Daniels' first touchdown and ignited a dominant second quarter. Florida State piled up 218 yards before halftime and carried a 17-7 lead into the locker room.

The Seminoles never let up. Daniels, Kromah and Micahi Danzy continued to attack a tiring Virginia defense. Danzy led all receivers with four catches for 70 yards, while Wisner added two receptions for 60 yards.

The offensive line created consistent running lanes throughout the night, though pass protection remains a concern. Daniels was sacked four times, and the unit committed multiple holding penalties.

Still, Florida State's most complete offensive outing of the season earns high marks.

After weeks of scrutiny, Florida State's defense delivered its best performance of the year.

The Seminoles held Virginia to just 206 total yards and only 37 rushing yards. The turning point came when back-to-back sacks by JuJu Wynn and Mandrell Desir energized the defense and completely shifted momentum. By halftime, Virginia had managed only minus-18 yards in the second quarter as Florida State took control.

The defensive front overwhelmed quarterback Beau Pribula from start to finish. The Cavaliers quarterback threw for 168 yards and a touchdown but spent much of the evening under relentless pressure. Florida State recorded 10 sacks, with Rylan Kennedy leading the way with two.

Chris Jones was disruptive throughout the game, frequently meeting ball carriers in the backfield and helping shut down key third- and fourth-down opportunities. Virginia converted just 3 of 15 third downs and failed on all four fourth-down attempts.

A late turnover capped a nearly flawless night for coordinator Tony White's defense.

The special teams unit delivered both encouraging moments and areas for continued improvement.

Punter Daniel Hughes showcased his leg strength with a booming 65-yard punt that pinned Virginia deep in its own territory. He averaged 47.2 yards across five punts and consistently flipped field position.

Jasen Lopez provided excitement in the return game, highlighted by a 31-yard punt return that nearly became a touchdown. However, consistency remains an issue. Lopez still must improve his decision-making when fielding punts and determining when to secure the ball versus letting it go.

Overall, the unit contributed positively but left room for growth.

Norvell and his staff deserve significant credit for how Florida State responded after a slow start.

The game plan emphasized physicality and aggression on both sides of the ball, and the players executed it effectively. Whatever message was delivered after the opening quarter clearly resonated, as the Seminoles dominated the remainder of the game.

Florida State played with confidence, and energy, producing its most complete performance against an FBS opponent this season.

This was exactly the type of performance Florida State needed heading into a challenging stretch of the schedule.

The Seminoles improved to 3-2, moved above .500 and earned their first conference victory. More importantly, they displayed an identity built around a powerful rushing attack and an aggressive defense capable of controlling games.

The next test will be whether Florida State can carry that momentum on the road against Louisville on a Friday night and Miami over the next two weeks. Those matchups will provide a clearer picture of where the Seminoles stand within the ACC hierarchy.

For now, though, Florida State has every reason to feel encouraged. The Seminoles played their most complete game of the season, and if they can replicate this level of execution, they may be positioned to make a strong run through October.

articles.title: Pitt QB Mason Heintschel's season is over after tearing the ACL in his right knee
articles.summary: PITTSBURGH (AP) — Pittsburgh sophomore quarterback Mason Heintschel is out for the rest of the season after tearing the ACL in his right knee in a victory ov...
articles.body:
PITTSBURGH (AP) — Pittsburgh sophomore quarterback Mason Heintschel is out for the rest of the season after tearing the ACL in his right knee in a victory over Virginia Tech on Friday night.

Pitt coach Pat Narduzzi made the announcement in a post on X on Saturday, about 24 hours after Heintschel was injured in the second half of what became a 35-33 win that boosted the Panthers' record to 5-0.

"We're heartbroken for Mason, but he's a resilient young man," Narduzzi wrote. "We know he'll attack his recovery with the same determination he brings to our building every day."

Heintschel was scrambling for yardage when he was tackled and fell to the ground with his right leg pinned behind him while simultaneously being hit by another Virginia Tech defender. He was in visible pain while being tended to by trainers and returned to the sideline later in the game on crutches.

Heintschel was off to an electric start for Pitt, throwing for 14 touchdowns against just one pick at the time of the injury.

Holden Gernier, a transfer from Auburn, came on for Heintschel and played well, throwing for 78 yards and a touchdown. Gernier figures to be the starter when Pitt (5-0, 2-0 ACC) hosts North Carolina (2-2, 0-1) at Acrisure Stadium on Oct. 10.

articles.title: Harper has punt- and FG-return TDs, Parson throws for 4 scores in Austin Peay's 42-17 win
articles.summary: (AP) — Denver Harper returned a punt and an off-line field-goal attempt for touchdowns and added another on one of Chris Parson's four TD passes in leading A...
articles.body:
CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Denver Harper returned a punt and an off-line field-goal attempt for touchdowns and added another on one of Chris Parson's four TD passes in leading Austin Peay to a 42-17 win over New Haven on Saturday.

Austin Peay took a 35-10 halftime lead after Harper reversed field and took a punt 82 yards for a TD then a few minutes later brought New Haven's 56-yard field-goal attempt deep out of the end zone and went the distance.

Parson threw three TD passes in the first half, a 10-yarder to Harper then a pair of catch-and-run TDs of 65 yards to Marvin Sims and 66 yards to Jaden Robinson. Parson connected with Ben Marshall for a 26-yard score in the fourth quarter.

Parson was 19 of 23 for 309 yards passing. Sims made six catches for 141 yards. The Governors (5-1), ranked No. 11 in the Stats Perform FCS Top 25, rushed for only 45 yards.

Niko Boyce was 25-of-39 passing for 227 yards and two touchdowns to Tommy Troy for the Chargers (1-5). Zaon Laney rushed for 90 yards on 17 carries.

Austin Peay: home against Tarleton State next Saturday

articles.title: 5 things you might've missed in UND's 55-28 win over Murray State

articles.body:
Oct. 3—GRAND FORKS — After trailing 21-0 early against Murray State, the No. 5 UND football team responded with 55 unanswered points in a 55-28 win over the Racers on Saturday during homecoming at the Alerus Center.

Here are five things you might've missed during the game.

Early in the third quarter, with UND holding a 31-21 lead, the Hawks picked up a key stop on third-and-7 against Murray State when Jonnie Wiltshire upended Racer wide receiver Trey Firestone short of the first down.

After the play, Wiltshire needed medical attention and was slow off the field.

"Jonnie is fine," UND head coach Eric Schmidt said. "He had maybe a contusion on his leg. I thought it was going to shoulder the way it looked initially, but it was lower body."

UND escaped the game relatively injury-free. UND edge Brody Thornton continued to battle a shoulder injury but isn't expected to miss any time long term.

UND shuffled the offensive line against Murray State due to an injury to Liam Becher at guard. Former starter Caleb Olson plugged into the spot.

The Hawks had a hard time, especially early in the game, protecting Kaminski.

Schmidt said UND's offensive line struggled with a little of everything early.

"It was communication things, and we got beat one-on-one," Schmidt said. "No. 15, and I hope he's okay, is a good edge player. We felt coming into the game he would be a handful."

No. 15, Jayden Walker, was injured late in the game but walked off after receiving medical attention.

"They were doing a good job denting the pocket," Schmidt said. "The edge players played with power on our tackles. They did a good job taking away our down-the-field. We had to be patient, which can be difficult when you're down early. It's easier to do that when you're up or the game is close."

UND's turnovers didn't help the defense early, but the Hawks still struggled to get Murray State off the field on drives.

The Racers' first score came after a 12-play drive. The third scoring drive was 16 plays.

"I think we tried to change up what we've been doing (schematically)," Schmidt said. "It was a little bit of the chess game, we probably were losing that early on just as far as not staying ahead of them with what they were doing."

Changing a defensive look became difficult early in the game with the quick turnovers.

"It was defensively just as much on me, but it gets hard when we're trying to sit down and talk ... then, hey, we have to talk the next time," Schmidt said of the turnovers impacting defensive changes. "It kind of snowballed. We're a team that's continuing to grind through some things here yet. By no means are we a finished product but there are some good signs of growth."

UND's Cameron Weir, a first-year transfer from Washington State, started the year with eight catches through the first four games.

He's had nine catches the last two weeks, including a career-high five grabs for 35 yards and a touchdown against Murray State. He added three punt returns for 71 yards, including a 57-yard touchdown in the first half to tie the game at 21-21.

"He's explosive," Schmidt said. "That's his superpower."

Weir's punt return touchdown was the first for the program since John Santiago had a 64-yard touchdown return against Portland State in 2017.

The Fighting Hawks' injury list has been growing recently but UND appears to be lined up to return to health next weekend at Northern Iowa.

All-American edge Lance Rucker practiced in pads this week but didnt' dress against the Racers. UND was also missing a number of starters or regulars including Becher, offensive lineman Ayden Teeter, tight end Hunter Kallstrom and safety Avery Dixon. Tight end Hadyn Stay warmed up but didn't see the field much.

"Stay was out there in a limited role today, but at least it was good to be able to get him back," Schmidt said. "I think Hunter Kallstrom coming back is going to be a shot in the arm, too. There's a couple of offensive lineman who progressed well this week who have a legitimate shot this week. You have to have a deep enough of a roster to weather those storms."

Schmidt said UND will evaluate Rucker this week to see if he can meet the next benchmark in his recovery from a preseason foot injury.
